passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: River Junior High School opened a new reading corner beside the school library. At first, some students thought it was just another quiet space. However, the reading corner soon became popular because students could borrow short books, magazines, and English comics during lunch break. The English teacher, Ms. Lin, also placed a suggestion box there. Students could write down topics they wanted to read about. After two weeks, the most popular topics were sports, animals, and travel. Ms. Lin said the reading corner was not only for strong readers. It was for anyone who wanted to build a small reading habit.

A teacher closed the school library during lunch.

passages.text: The school volleyball team lost its first game of the season. After the game, Coach Wang did not blame the players. Instead, he asked them to watch a video of the match and write down one thing they did well and one thing they needed to improve. Most players noticed that they missed many serves in the second half. The team decided to add a short serving practice before every regular practice. Three weeks later, the players felt more confident. They still made mistakes, but they were no longer afraid of serving during important points.

items.title: Storm Notes for June

items.source: NOAA Climate Prediction Center Atlantic Hurricane Outlook; https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/hurricane.shtml?vm=r; accessed 2026-06-01
items.usage: 依 NOAA 2026 大西洋颶風季展望重寫短文與圖表，用於題材與數字查證，未直接複製原文。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: At school, Kevin helped the science club make a June safety poster. He read NOAA's outlook for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and learned that a below-normal season was the most likely result. Still, his teacher reminded everyone that below-normal does not mean danger-free. A single strong storm can still cause serious flooding, power cuts, and travel problems. Kevin added three simple tips to the poster: check weather updates, prepare flashlights and water, and talk with family members about where to go in an emergency. He also wrote that the Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, so students should stay alert for many months, not only during one stormy week.

passages.label: Chart
passages.text: 2026 Atlantic outlook: below-normal season 55%; near-normal season 35%; above-normal season 10%. Expected ranges: 8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes, 1-3 major hurricanes.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Kevin used hurricane-season information to help make a school safety poster.
Kevin decided to travel during every storm.
The science club canceled all summer activities.
The teacher said storms never cause real problems.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on Kevin reading the outlook and turning it into a safety poster.

questions.question: When does the Atlantic hurricane season officially run?
questions.explanation: Passage A states that the season officially runs from June 1 to November 30.

questions.question: According to the chart, what is the expected range for named storms?
questions.explanation: The chart says the expected range is 8-14 named storms.

questions.question: Why did Kevin's teacher still want students to prepare for emergencies?
options: Because even one strong storm can still be dangerous.
Because NOAA said storms would never end.
Because the club wanted to sell flashlights.
Because school would stay closed for six months.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that below-normal does not mean there is no danger.

questions.question: What does "outlook" most likely mean in this passage?
questions.explanation: NOAA's outlook refers to its seasonal forecast.

questions.question: What does "it" refer to in "it officially runs from June 1 to November 30"?
questions.explanation: "It" refers to the Atlantic hurricane season.

questions.question: Which statement is supported by both the passage and the chart?

The season has a 55% chance of being above-normal.
questions.explanation: The chart shows only probabilities, and the passage explains why people should still prepare.

questions.question: Which season outcome is most likely in the chart? Brief answer: Give one reason Kevin still included emergency tips.
questions.sample_brief_answer: He still included them because a single strong storm can cause serious damage even in a below-normal season.
questions.explanation: The chart gives below-normal the highest probability, and Passage A explains the safety reason.

items.source: NASA Science article on asteroid 2024 YR4; https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/planetary-defense/2026/03/05/new-nasa-asteroid-observations-eliminate-chance-of-2032-lunar-impact/; accessed 2026-06-01
items.usage: 依 NASA 對 2024 YR4 的最新觀測結果重寫科普短文與時間線，用於事實查證與題材設計，未直接複製原文。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: During science class, Ms. Huang showed students a short update about asteroid 2024 YR4. New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope helped NASA refine the asteroid's path. The new data showed that the asteroid is expected to pass the Moon on December 22, 2032, at a distance of about 13,200 miles. NASA also said the object poses no significant risk to Earth. Ms. Huang told the class that this was a good example of how science works: experts make early estimates, collect more evidence, and improve their answers. The students agreed that the most important lesson was not to panic when a first report sounds uncertain.

passages.label: Passage B
passages.text: Timeline Note: Early 2025 reports said 2024 YR4 had a small but notable chance of hitting Earth. By March 2026, after more observations, NASA ruled out a lunar impact and said the asteroid no longer posed a significant Earth threat.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: New observations helped scientists better understand an asteroid's path.
Students discovered a new asteroid by themselves.
NASA warned people to leave Earth at once.
The Moon changed its orbit suddenly.
questions.explanation: The passage is about better data leading to a clearer understanding of the asteroid.

questions.question: About how far from the Moon is 2024 YR4 expected to pass in 2032?
questions.explanation: Passage A gives the distance as about 13,200 miles.

questions.question: Why did Ms. Huang say students should not panic about the first report?
options: Because early reports can change when scientists get more evidence.
Because NASA never studies space objects carefully.
Because the class was not interested in science.
questions.explanation: The passage says science improves answers with more evidence.

questions.question: What does "refine" most likely mean in Passage A?
questions.explanation: NASA refined the path by making its prediction more exact.

questions.question: What does "this" refer to in "this was a good example of how science works"?
options: the process of improving predictions with more evidence
questions.explanation: "This" refers to the process Ms. Huang just described.

questions.question: What does the sentence "experts make early estimates, collect more evidence, and improve their answers" mean?
options: Scientific conclusions can become more accurate over time.
Answers should stay the same even if facts change.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains that science becomes more accurate as new data arrives.

questions.question: Which statement matches both passages?
options: Later observations reduced the earlier concern about 2024 YR4.
The asteroid is now expected to hit Earth in 2032.
Students were told to ignore new evidence.
questions.explanation: Both passages explain that later data lowered the risk.

questions.question: Which tool helped provide the new observations? Brief answer: What bigger lesson did Ms. Huang want students to learn?
questions.sample_brief_answer: She wanted them to learn that scientific answers improve when new evidence is collected.
questions.explanation: Passage A names the telescope, and the lesson is explained directly.

passages.text: Future spacecraft may need to refuel in Earth orbit before traveling farther into space. passages.text: ESA’s Euclid mission created a very large visible-light image of the center of the Milky Way. The image was captured on March 23, 2025, in about 26 hours and was made from nine camera pointings. Each pointing covered an area larger than the full Moon in the sky. passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: Earth receives energy from the Sun. Some sunlight warms the ground and oceans. Later, Earth sends part of that energy back toward space as heat. Certain gases in the atmosphere slow some of this escaping heat, so the air near the ground stays warmer. This natural process is called the greenhouse effect. Without it, Earth would be much colder. However, when people add more heat-trapping gases by burning coal, oil, and gas, the blanket around Earth becomes thicker. Then more heat stays near the surface, and the average temperature can rise. Scientists study this process to explain why small changes in the atmosphere can affect weather, oceans, farms, and daily life.

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: On a windy afternoon, a lifeguard noticed a narrow line of choppy water moving away from the beach. She raised a yellow flag and used a speaker to warn swimmers. Fighting straight against it can make a person tired quickly. Beach safety teachers tell swimmers to stay calm, float if they need rest, and swim parallel to the beach until they are out of the current. Then they can swim back toward land. The lifeguard also reminded visitors to check warning flags before entering the water.

items.title: Moving More, Sitting Less
items.topic: 健康生活、運動習慣、資訊整合
items.usage: 依 WHO physical activity fact sheet 改寫學生版健康閱讀，保留規律身體活動有助健康、久坐需減少、不同年齡可用適合自己的方式增加活動量等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: Jin used to sit after school for three hours and then complain that he felt tired. His aunt, a nurse, did not tell him to become an athlete. She suggested a small plan: walk home twice a week, stretch for five minutes after homework, and play basketball with friends on Saturday. Jin was surprised that physical activity did not have to mean a long race or a difficult gym class. It could be walking, playing, dancing, or doing active chores. After two weeks, he still enjoyed games on his tablet, but he also noticed that short movement breaks helped him feel more awake.

passages.label: Activity Log
passages.text: Monday: walked home, 18 minutes. Tuesday: no activity break. Wednesday: stretched, 5 minutes. Thursday: helped carry recycling, 10 minutes. Saturday: basketball, 35 minutes.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Small kinds of physical activity can help a student move more.
Jin becomes a professional basketball player.
A nurse tells Jin to stop all hobbies.
Tablet games are the only way to feel awake.
questions.explanation: The passage shows Jin adding simple activities to his week.

questions.question: Who suggested the small activity plan?
questions.explanation: The passage says his aunt, a nurse, suggested the plan.

questions.question: Why was Jin surprised?
options: He learned that activity could include simple daily movement.
He thought walking home was impossible.
He had never seen a basketball.
questions.explanation: He realized physical activity could be walking, playing, dancing, or chores.

questions.question: What does "chores" most likely mean?
questions.explanation: Carrying recycling is an example of an active chore.

questions.question: What does "It" refer to in "It could be walking, playing, dancing"?
questions.explanation: The previous sentence discusses physical activity.

questions.question: What does the aunt's advice suggest?
options: Students can begin with realistic activities instead of extreme exercise.
Sitting all day is always healthy.
Exercise must happen only in a gym.
questions.explanation: Her plan uses short, simple activities that fit Jin's life.

questions.question: According to the Activity Log, when did Jin play basketball?
questions.explanation: The log lists basketball on Saturday for 35 minutes.

questions.question: Which activity took 18 minutes? Brief answer: What is one simple movement break Jin tried?
questions.sample_brief_answer: He stretched for five minutes or helped carry recycling.
questions.explanation: The Activity Log says Monday's walk home took 18 minutes.

items.title: Looking at an Eclipse Safely
items.topic: 天文觀察、安全規則、多文本整合
items.usage: 依 NASA eclipse viewing safety 官方資訊改寫，保留不可直接看太陽、需使用合格太陽觀測眼鏡或間接觀測、普通太陽眼鏡不安全等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: The science club planned to watch a solar eclipse from the school yard. Mr. Chen first collected the students' regular sunglasses and placed them in a box. Some students laughed, but he explained that ordinary sunglasses are not made for looking at the Sun. The club used special eclipse glasses and also built a simple pinhole viewer from cardboard. With the viewer, students did not look at the Sun directly. They watched a small image of the Sun appear on white paper. The event felt exciting because everyone could enjoy it without risking their eyes.

passages.label: Safety Rules
passages.text: 1. Do not look directly at the Sun without proper solar viewing protection. 2. Regular sunglasses are not eclipse glasses. 3. A pinhole viewer lets you watch an image of the Sun indirectly. 4. Stop using damaged viewing glasses.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Students learn safe ways to watch a solar eclipse.
Students buy new sunglasses for a fashion show.
A club cancels science class forever.
Mr. Chen teaches students how to draw cartoons.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on eclipse safety methods.

questions.question: What did Mr. Chen collect first?
questions.explanation: The passage says he collected regular sunglasses and put them in a box.

questions.question: Why did Mr. Chen collect the regular sunglasses?
options: He wanted to prevent students from using unsafe eye protection.
He wanted to sell the sunglasses.
He needed cardboard for a viewer.
He did not want students to go outside.
questions.explanation: He explains ordinary sunglasses are not safe for looking at the Sun.

questions.question: What does "indirectly" most likely mean in the Safety Rules?
questions.explanation: A pinhole viewer lets students see an image instead of looking straight at the Sun.

questions.question: What does "them" refer to in "placed them in a box"?
questions.explanation: The sentence says he collected the students' regular sunglasses.

questions.question: What does the final sentence suggest?
options: Safety rules helped students enjoy the event.
The eclipse was boring for everyone.
questions.explanation: The final sentence says students enjoyed the event without risking their eyes.

questions.question: Which idea appears in both Passage A and the Safety Rules?
options: Regular sunglasses are not safe for eclipse viewing.
Every student must buy a telescope.
The club watches the Moon indoors.
questions.explanation: Both texts warn that regular sunglasses are not proper eclipse protection.

questions.question: What can a pinhole viewer show? Brief answer: Name one unsafe action from the Safety Rules.
questions.sample_brief_answer: Looking directly at the Sun without proper solar viewing protection is unsafe.
questions.explanation: The rules say a pinhole viewer lets people watch an image of the Sun indirectly.

items.title: The Cooling Center Plan
items.topic: 高溫安全、社區公告、公共資訊判讀
items.source: National Weather Service: Heat Safety Tips and Resources
items.usage: 依 NWS heat safety 官方資料改寫社區高溫安全短文與公告，保留高溫可能造成健康風險、需照顧易受影響族群、避免把兒童或寵物留在車內等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: During a very hot week, Maple Town opened the school gym as a cooling center. The mayor asked volunteers to call older neighbors, families with young children, and people who lived alone. At the center, visitors could drink water, rest under fans, and charge their phones. The town also sent a short warning: never leave children or pets inside a parked car, even for a few minutes. Lina first thought heat safety was only about feeling uncomfortable. After helping at the center, she understood that heat can make some health problems worse and that checking on others can be part of staying safe.

passages.label: Notice
passages.text: Cooling Center Hours: Monday to Friday, 10:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. Bring a water bottle if you can. Volunteers will make check-in calls at 2:00 p.m. each day.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: A town uses a cooling center and neighbor checks to respond to extreme heat.
A school gym closes because no one needs it.
Lina learns how to repair electric fans.
The mayor cancels all phone calls in town.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on heat safety actions in the community.

questions.question: Where did Maple Town open the cooling center?
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the school gym became a cooling center.

questions.question: Why did volunteers call older neighbors and people living alone?
options: They might need help during extreme heat.
They were selling fans door to door.
They wanted everyone to attend a concert.
They needed people to teach math.
questions.explanation: The calls help check on people who may be more affected by heat.

questions.question: What does "charge" mean in the Notice context?
options: put power into a phone battery
questions.explanation: Visitors can charge their phones at the center, meaning add battery power.

questions.question: What does "she" refer to in the final sentence?
questions.explanation: The previous sentence names Lina as the person who learned from helping.

questions.question: What does Lina understand by the end of the passage?
options: Heat safety includes caring for people who may be at higher risk.
Only athletes need to drink water.
Cooling centers are used only in winter.
questions.explanation: The final sentence links heat risk with checking on others.

questions.question: According to the Notice, when do volunteers make check-in calls?
questions.explanation: The Notice says calls happen at 2:00 p.m. each day.

questions.question: Which action is warned against in Passage A? Brief answer: Name one service offered at the cooling center.
options: Leaving children or pets inside a parked car.
questions.sample_brief_answer: Visitors can drink water, rest under fans, or charge phones.
questions.explanation: The warning says not to leave children or pets in a parked car.

items.title: The No-Waste Lunch Week
items.topic: 環境教育、食物浪費、計畫與表格閱讀
items.source: US EPA: Preventing Wasted Food At Home
items.usage: 依 EPA reducing wasted food at home 官方頁面改寫學生版環境閱讀，保留美國約三分之一食物未被食用、規劃餐點、先檢查冰箱與保存剩食等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: Class 8B started a No-Waste Lunch Week after learning that a large amount of food is never eaten. Their teacher did not ask everyone to bring tiny lunches. Instead, students learned to plan better. Before shopping, they checked what was already in the refrigerator. They wrote a simple menu, packed only the amount they could finish, and saved clean leftovers for the next day. By Friday, the trash bin beside their classroom was not empty, but it was much lighter. The class learned that preventing waste can begin before food reaches the lunch box.

passages.label: Lunch Check Table
passages.text: Monday: 12 unfinished sandwiches. Wednesday: 5 unfinished sandwiches. Friday: 2 unfinished sandwiches. Best student idea: label leftovers with the date.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Students reduce lunch waste by planning and using leftovers wisely.
Students stop eating lunch at school.
A teacher asks students to buy more food every day.
questions.explanation: The passage describes practical ways to prevent food waste.

questions.question: What did students check before shopping?
options: What was already in the refrigerator.
The number of desks in class.
questions.explanation: The passage says they checked the refrigerator before shopping.

questions.question: Why did the trash bin become much lighter by Friday?
options: The trash bin was moved outside.
No one ate lunch that week.
The school bought a new bin.
questions.explanation: The project reduced unfinished food, so less went into the bin.

questions.question: What does "leftovers" most likely mean?
options: food that remains after a meal
questions.explanation: The students saved clean leftovers for the next day.

questions.question: What does "it" refer to in "it was much lighter"?
questions.explanation: The sentence says the trash bin was not empty but was lighter.

questions.question: What does "preventing waste can begin before food reaches the lunch box" mean?
options: Planning and shopping choices can reduce waste later.
Students should never cook at home.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes planning before packing lunch.

questions.question: According to the Lunch Check Table, how many unfinished sandwiches were recorded on Friday?
questions.explanation: The table lists 2 unfinished sandwiches on Friday.

questions.question: Which student idea helps people remember when food was saved? Brief answer: Name one planning step from Passage A.
questions.sample_brief_answer: They checked the refrigerator, wrote a menu, or packed only what they could finish.
questions.explanation: The table says the best idea was labeling leftovers with the date.

items.title: Tiny Plastic, Big Questions
items.topic: 海洋保育、微塑膠、分類與推論
items.usage: 依 NOAA Marine Debris Program 微塑膠頁面改寫短文，保留 primary/secondary microplastics、塑膠碎裂來源、海灘清理與源頭減量等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: After a beach cleanup, Mei found many bright plastic pieces smaller than a grain of rice. Her group learned that tiny plastic pieces can come from two paths. Some are made small on purpose, such as plastic pellets used to make larger products. Others begin as bottles, bags, or toys and break apart after sunlight, heat, wind, and waves make the plastic weak. The students could not remove every tiny piece from the sand, so their report suggested two actions: pick up larger trash before it breaks and use fewer single-use plastic items at school events.

passages.label: Sort Cards
passages.text: Card 1: plastic pellet used in a factory. Card 2: bottle cap broken by waves. Card 3: foam cup pieces found near a picnic table. Card 4: reusable water station at sports day.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Tiny plastic pieces can come from different sources, so prevention matters.
Plastic pieces are easy to count perfectly.
Mei opens a toy shop near the beach.
Students learn that all beach sand is plastic.
questions.explanation: The passage explains sources of microplastics and prevention ideas.

questions.question: What did Mei find after the beach cleanup?
options: Many bright plastic pieces smaller than a grain of rice.
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes the tiny pieces she found.

questions.question: Why did the students suggest picking up larger trash early?
options: Large plastic can break into smaller pieces later.
Large trash becomes school supplies overnight.
Beach trash always disappears by itself.
Waves turn plastic into fresh water.
questions.explanation: The passage says bottles, bags, and toys can break apart over time.

questions.question: What does "single-use" most likely mean?
options: made to be used once and then thrown away
used by only one teacher forever
questions.explanation: Single-use plastic items are contrasted with prevention and waste reduction.

questions.question: What does "Others" refer to in the sentence about bottles, bags, or toys?
options: tiny plastic pieces from a second path
questions.explanation: The previous sentence introduces two paths for tiny plastic pieces.

questions.question: What does the report suggest about microplastics?
options: It is better to prevent plastic waste before it becomes tiny.
The best solution is to ignore small pieces.
Factories should make more plastic pellets for beaches.
Students can clean all sand perfectly in one day.
questions.explanation: The suggested actions focus on prevention and reducing plastic use.

questions.question: Which Sort Card is the best example of preventing future plastic waste?
options: Card 4: reusable water station at sports day.
Card 1: plastic pellet used in a factory.
Card 2: bottle cap broken by waves.
Card 3: foam cup pieces found near a picnic table.
questions.explanation: A reusable water station reduces the need for single-use plastic.

questions.question: Which card is closest to a primary microplastic example? Brief answer: Give one source of secondary microplastics.
questions.sample_brief_answer: A bottle, bag, toy, cap, or foam cup can break into smaller pieces.
questions.explanation: A plastic pellet made small for manufacturing is closest to a primary microplastic example.

items.title: Mina Changes Her Passwords
items.topic: 數位安全、強密碼、生活決策
items.source: CISA Secure Our World: Use Strong Passwords
items.usage: 依 CISA 強密碼官方建議改寫校園數位安全短文，保留密碼應 long、random、unique，可用 password manager，避免生日與寵物名等易猜資訊。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: Mina used the same short password for her game account, school email, and photo app. It included her dog’s name and birthday, so she could remember it easily. During Digital Safety Week, a speaker compared weak passwords to a locked door with the key still in the lock. Mina changed her plan. She made each important account use a different password. The new passwords were longer and not based on personal facts. She also asked her parents about using a password manager, so she would not need to memorize every random string.

passages.label: Password Notes
passages.text: Old password clue: pet name + birthday. New rule: long + random + unique. Tool to consider: password manager. Account list: school email, game account, photo app.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: Mina learns to replace weak repeated passwords with stronger ones.
Mina teaches her dog to use email.
A speaker tells students to stop using all accounts.
The school cancels Digital Safety Week.
questions.explanation: The passage shows Mina changing weak password habits.

questions.question: What personal facts did Mina’s old password include?
options: A train number and city map.
questions.explanation: The passage says the old password included her dog’s name and birthday.

questions.question: Why might using the same password for many accounts be risky?
options: One stolen password could help someone enter several accounts.
It makes every account too colorful.
It prevents Mina from taking photos.
It makes passwords impossible to type.
questions.explanation: If the same password is reused, one problem can affect multiple accounts.

questions.question: What does "unique" most likely mean in the Password Notes?
questions.explanation: Unique passwords are different for each account.

questions.question: What does "it" refer to in "she could remember it easily"?
questions.explanation: The sentence describes Mina’s old password and why it was easy to remember.

questions.question: What does the speaker’s door comparison suggest?
options: A password can look protective but still be unsafe if it is easy to guess.
Every door at school needs a new color.
Keys are better than computers for all learning.
Students should keep passwords on a desk.
questions.explanation: The comparison warns that weak passwords do not protect accounts well.

questions.question: Which Password Notes rule matches Mina’s new plan in Passage A?
questions.explanation: The passage says her new passwords were longer, not personal, and different.

questions.question: Which tool might help Mina manage many passwords? Brief answer: Name one account from the notes.
questions.sample_brief_answer: One account is school email, the game account, or the photo app.
questions.explanation: The passage and notes both mention a password manager.

items.title: A Laboratory Above Earth
items.topic: 太空站、國際合作、研究平台
items.source: NASA: International Space Station reference page
items.usage: 依 NASA International Space Station reference page 改寫科普閱讀，保留太空站是國際合作研究平台、2000 年起持續有人居住、微重力實驗室、足球場大小與 2030 年前後研究任務等概念。

passages.label: Passage A
passages.text: When Leo heard the words space station, he imagined a quiet hotel above Earth. His science teacher gave the class a better picture: the International Space Station is an orbiting research laboratory built through international cooperation. Since people first began living there continuously in 2000, astronauts and partners from many countries have used the station for experiments that are difficult to do on Earth. In microgravity, objects and fluids behave differently, so researchers can test technology, study health, and learn more about living in space. Leo wrote in his notebook, "It is not a hotel; it is a classroom, workshop, and laboratory above Earth."

passages.label: Fact Box
passages.text: First continuous crew: 2000. Main role: research platform in space. Size comparison: about the size of a football field. Visitors: astronauts and space travelers from many countries.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Passage A?
options: The International Space Station is a cooperative research laboratory above Earth.
Leo books a vacation hotel in space.
A teacher asks students to play football in class.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the station as a research platform, not a hotel.

questions.question: When did people begin living continuously on the station?
questions.explanation: Both the passage and Fact Box mention 2000.

questions.question: Why are some experiments useful to do on the station?
options: Microgravity lets researchers observe things that behave differently from on Earth.
All experiments need a football field.
questions.explanation: The passage says objects and fluids behave differently in microgravity.

questions.question: What does "cooperation" most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The station is built and used by international partners.

questions.question: What does "there" refer to in "living there continuously"?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about people living on the station.

questions.question: What does Leo mean by calling the station a classroom, workshop, and laboratory?
options: People learn, build, and study there.
The station is only for sleeping.
Students take regular school buses there.
The station is a sports stadium.
questions.explanation: His description summarizes learning, technology work, and research.

questions.question: Which order best matches the ideas in Passage A?
options: Leo imagines a hotel -> teacher explains the station -> experiments in microgravity -> Leo writes a new idea.
Experiments in microgravity -> Leo writes a new idea -> teacher cancels class -> Leo imagines a hotel.
Teacher explains the station -> football game begins -> Leo sleeps -> astronauts leave Earth forever.
Leo writes a new idea -> station is built underwater -> class starts a beach cleanup -> hotel opens.
questions.explanation: This option follows the passage from misunderstanding to corrected understanding.

questions.question: According to the Fact Box, what is the station about the size of? Brief answer: Name one kind of work researchers can do there.
questions.sample_brief_answer: Researchers can test technology, study health, or learn about living in space.
questions.explanation: The Fact Box gives the football field size comparison.
